news.title: FBI blames North Korea for stealing $6.3B from Binance in biggest crypto heist in history
news.text:
The theft of billions of dollars from Binance within a matter of minutes, the biggest crypto heist in history, was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, the FBI said Saturday.

The bureau said in a statement that this week’s attack was tied to “malicious cyber activity” by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.

The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins.

It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called Ethereum.

The FBI expects that TraderTraitor will now attempt to convert the assets using DeFi and “instant swap services.”

Asked by reporters as he appeared on Saturday night during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, however, President Donald Trump suggested investigators weren’t yet certain that North Korea was involved.

“I’m not concerned. We’re learning about it,” Trump said of the case. “We don’t know if it’s North Korea.” Though he added that, it could yet be determined that it was.

Crypto expert Ari Redbord said he expects the hackers will break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them through smaller exchanges to evade detection, a process that could unfold over months.

“It’s bank robbery, in this case, at the speed of the Internet,” said Redbord, chief policy officer at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs. “However, we can also track and trace those funds in real time in order to build investigations, to disrupt and to seize back funds.”

He added: “It’s just this cat and mouse game.”

On Thursday, $6.3 billion in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, in what several crypto experts said bore the hallmarks of a North Korean hack.

The company said Saturday that it had enough set aside in the same digital currency that was stolen to cover 90% of the missing assets and promised that customers would be fully reimbursed.
news.summary: The theft of billions of dollars from Binance within a matter of minutes, the biggest crypto heist in history, was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, the FBI said Saturday.

Israel’s economic outlook is extraordinary.

news.title: Elissa Slotkin Shows That More Democrat Lawfare Is Coming
news.text:
You’re not supposed to say the quiet part out loud, but that’s what Elissa Slotkin just did. The U.S. senator from Michigan promised that Democrats would investigate the Trump administration to intimidate young conservatives from going into politics.

“I want them to be like, ‘Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want, and so let me avoid participating in that,’” she said. “I want that deterrence message.”

Yes, the party of the West Wing is now trying to terrorize idealists out of going to Washington. Conservatives understandably are furious over Slotkin’s comments, yet she only doubled down, calling the outrage “manufactured.”

Just as important as their baldfaced cynicism is what Slotkin’s remarks tell us about a likely Democrat Congress after November. By promising to use investigations as a tool of raw power, Slotkin revealed that Democrats’ agenda will begin and end with one word: lawfare.

This isn’t anything new. The last time the Left controlled the White House, under Joe Biden, government agencies like the Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission were coopted for political ends.

The clearest example was the FBI investigation codenamed, in ridiculous Michael Bay style, Arctic Frost. Led by Jack Smith, the Bureau launched a broad-ranging probe into Donald Trump along with more than 90 Republican figures and organizations, including Turning Point USA and the Republican National Committee.

Imagine that, immediately after taking the oath of office, Trump had put the Democratic National Committee under investigation, and you understand how serious this is. Yet unleashing federal law enforcement on the whole of the Republican Right didn’t trouble the Biden brigades one bit.

Neither did the Biden DOJ’s weaponization of the FACE Act to target Catholic pro-lifers, whom one federal prosecutor described as “culty.” Mark Houck, a pro-life activist, had his house invaded by a SWAT team and was arrested in front of his kids.

Also not troubling to Democrats was how the Biden team leveraged antitrust law to go after capitalism, punishing companies they didn’t like for the mere act of existing. The dragnet was so wide that at one point not just problem actors like Big Tech but 40 percent of companies under the S&P market cap were being scrutinized by the DOJ, leading The Wall Street Journal to declare “everyone is under investigation.”

Yet the cherry on top of the lawfare sundae wasn’t who was prosecuted but who wasn’t. Namely, Joe Biden’s son, Hunter, who received one of the broadest presidential pardons in American history right before his father left office.

Since they were vanquished by Trump in 2024, the Left’s legal persecutors haven’t slowed down. Democrat state attorneys general and interest groups have formed a kind of shadow DOJ, launching more than 370 active legal cases against the Trump administration.

The anti-business commissars are also still afoot. Biden’s former chief antitrust cop, Lina Khan, got a plum teaching position at Columbia Law School and still issues anti-business edicts on X. Many of her former staffers coalesced into groups like the American Economic Liberties Project, which push a thinly veiled socialist agenda.

These guys are salivating at the prospect of reentering government. If the Democrats win in 2026 and 2028, they’ll get their chance.

Their incoming lawfare is being plotted out in the open. Should they retake Congress, Democrats say they plan to investigate the president’s family personally and crack down on his law enforcement efforts against illegal immigration.

Slotkin’s comments show this isn’t just about “get Trump” (though there’s that). Democrats are also aiming to intimidate, whether it’s the Trump administration, Republican commentators, or young conservatives who are thinking about a career in public service.

Lawfare is now a feature, maybe the feature, of Democrat governance. It’s time to say no to more investigations run amok.

Bob Barr represented Georgia’s Seventh District in the U.S. House of Representatives from 1995 to 2003. He served previously as the United States Attorney in Atlanta from 1986 to 1990 and was an official with the CIA in the 1970s. He now practices law in Atlanta, Georgia, serves as head of Liberty Guard, and is the immediate past president of the National Rifle Association of America.

 Hamilton grabs pole position for Mexican Grand Prix 







MEXICO CITY, Mexico (AFP) — Lewis Hamilton edged George Russell on Saturday to take pole position for the Mexican Grand Prix.

As Hamilton grabbed his first pole position since 2023, his Ferrari teammate Charles Leclerc was third while championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who only needs to finish ninth on Sunday to ensure he clinches the world title, was fifth fastest in his Mercedes.

The Italian will start from fourth because Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, who was fourth fastest, had already been handed a one-place grid penalty for a collision with Liam Lawson in practice on Friday.

Hamilton recorded a fastest time of 1 minute 16.514 seconds to edgeRussell of Mercedes by 0.009sec with Leclerc at 0.119.

“Wow. That felt great. That feels good,” said Hamilton after becoming, at 41, the oldest man to grab a Grand Prix pole since Mario Andretti in 1982.

“I think this is my first pole with Ferrari, and 105, I like that number. Where there’s a will, there’s a way.”

 ‘An Abominable Betrayal’: Patterson blasts Jamaica’s abstention on Cuba 







Former Prime Minister PJ Patterson has slammed the Holness administration’s decision to abstain from voting on the United Nations resolution calling for an end to the embargo against Cuba as “an abominable betrayal which history will never forget”.

The vote marked a shift in policy by Jamaica as historically the island has voted “yes” in favour of ending the United States economic, commercial and financial embargo against Cuba for over 30 years since the annual UN resolution began.

In a scathing rebuke of the decision by Jamaica, Patterson said “It was a day of shame for the land of Marcus Garvey, and a stain on the record of a nation which, before we had even raised our own flag, closed its ports to trade with apartheid South Africa.”

Patterson recalled that in December 1972, he accompanied then Prime Minister Michael Manley to the meeting at which four newly independent Caribbean states resolved to establish diplomatic relations with Cuba, “defying the isolation others sought to impose.”

He said, “We took that decision not because it was easy, but because it was right, and because we understood that the sovereignty we had so recently won would mean little if we allowed others to choose our friends, least of all a friend that is our closest neighbour.”

Noting that he is the last surviving participant in that decision, Patterson said: “I write with a sense of agony and seething outrage that Jamaica could so suddenly abandon the fundamental tenets on which it rested: the sovereign equality of states, non-interference in their domestic jurisdiction, and the right of every people to self-determination free from external threat or coercion.”

Patterson was among 11 former Heads of Government of the Caribbean Community who, four days before the UN vote, issued statements urging global support for an end to the US embargo against Cuba.

“We said then, and I repeat now, that the embargo is contrary to international law, that it violates Cuba’s sovereignty and the most elemental rights of its people, and that the pressures being deployed to defeat the resolution must be resisted,” Patterson said. “Former Prime Minister Bruce Golding signed that letter alongside me. On this crucial matter, Jamaica’s former leaders spoke with one voice. The present Government has chosen silence.”

Patterson challenged Foreign Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith’s explanation that the “Government had been reflecting on the matter for some time, that the abstention represents a shift in policy, and that the resolution left no scope to reflect the broader context the Government wished to see.”

READ: Shift in policy

According to the former prime minister, “That explanation does not withstand scrutiny.

“If there was no external pressure, as the Government insists, then it must explain how a fundamental reversal of a policy pursued by every Administration since 1992 serves Jamaica’s best interest. It must also explain why it was never brought to parliament if this reflection had been under way for some time,” he said.

Patterson also accused the government of flouting Parliament’s constitutional authority, noting that the vote came less than 24 hours after the House of Representatives passed, without dissent, a resolution on the economic and humanitarian situation in Cuba. 

“It was the Government’s own resolution, brought to the House by the minister of state in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs,” Patterson said. “In moving it, he declared that Jamaica could not support a unilaterally imposed blockade against Cuba. The resolution called for efforts to reduce the economic restrictions on Cuba and to facilitate its progressive integration into the international economic system, rather than its isolation under a blockade.”

Patterson argued, “Our abstention violated the unanimous decision of the Legislature. It was a deplorable flouting of Parliament’s constitutional authority, the highest expression of the will of the people in our democracy.

“Members on both sides of the House were led to believe one thing on Tuesday and confronted with its opposite on Wednesday. This is no mere discourtesy. It was an act of deception and a grave parliamentary offence,” the former prime minister continued in his rebuke. “In any Parliament modelled on Westminster, what took place between Tuesday and Wednesday would have resulted in censure and ministerial resignations. The Parliament of Jamaica is entitled to no less. It was an abominable betrayal which history will never forget.”

See full statement by PJ Patterson below.

On Wednesday, 28 October 2026, Jamaica abstained when the United Nations General Assembly voted on the resolution calling for an end to the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States against Cuba. For more than three decades, under every Administration since the resolution was first tabled in 1992, Jamaica voted yes. We did so under governments of both parties, because the yes vote was never partisan. It was a matter of principle.

It was a day of shame for the land of Marcus Garvey, and a stain on the record of a nation which, before we had even raised our own flag, closed its ports to trade with apartheid South Africa. That was an unequivocal declaration that the Jamaican people, though a small nation, would not support the oppression of others. On Wednesday, Jamaica’s Government trampled that tradition. It was an abominable betrayal which history will never forget.

In December 1972, I accompanied Prime Minister Michael Manley to the meeting at which four newly independent Caribbean states resolved to establish diplomatic relations with Cuba, defying the isolation others sought to impose. We took that decision not because it was easy, but because it was right, and because we understood that the sovereignty we had so recently won would mean little if we allowed others to choose our friends, least of all a friend that is our closest neighbour.

I am the last surviving participant in that decision, and I write with a sense of agony and seething outrage that Jamaica could so suddenly abandon the fundamental tenets on which it rested: the sovereign equality of states, non-interference in their domestic jurisdiction, and the right of every people to self-determination free from external threat or coercion.

Four days before the UN vote, eleven of my fellow former Heads of Government of the Caribbean Community and I wrote to all the nations of the world urging support for the resolution. We said then, and I repeat now, that the embargo is contrary to international law, that it violates Cuba’s sovereignty and the most elemental rights of its people, and that the pressures being deployed to defeat the resolution must be resisted. Former Prime Minister Bruce Golding signed that letter alongside me. On this crucial matter, Jamaica’s former leaders spoke with one voice. The present Government has chosen silence.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs tells us that the Government had been reflecting on this matter for some time, that the abstention represents a shift in policy, and that the resolution left no scope to reflect the broader context the Government wished to see. That explanation does not withstand scrutiny.

If there was no external pressure, as the Government insists, then it must explain how a fundamental reversal of a policy pursued by every Administration since 1992 serves Jamaica’s best interest. It must also explain why it was never brought to parliament if this reflection had been under way for some time.

On Tuesday, 27 October, the House of Representatives passed, without dissent, a resolution on the economic and humanitarian situation in Cuba. It was the Government’s own resolution, brought to the House by the Minister of State in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. In moving it, he declared that Jamaica could not support a unilaterally imposed blockade against Cuba. The resolution called for efforts to reduce the economic restrictions on Cuba and to facilitate its progressive integration into the international economic system, rather than its isolation under a blockade.

Within twenty-four hours, Jamaica abstained. Our abstention violated the unanimous decision of the Legislature. It was a deplorable flouting of Parliament’s constitutional authority, the highest expression of the will of the people in our democracy.

Members on both sides of the House were led to believe one thing on Tuesday and confronted with its opposite on Wednesday. This is no mere discourtesy. It was an act of deception and a grave parliamentary offence. In any Parliament modelled on Westminster, what took place between Tuesday and Wednesday would have resulted in censure and ministerial resignations. The Parliament of Jamaica is entitled to no less. It was an abominable betrayal which history will never forget.

The Minister of State’s own words explain precisely why we should have voted yes. Small states have no mighty army to defend us, and insufficient economic weight to shield us against the exercise of military might and power. Our security rests on the international rule of law and on a credible multilateral system with the Charter of the United Nations at its centre. When a powerful nation imposes its will unilaterally on a small neighbour, and we do not object, we weaken the very shield on which our own sovereignty depends.

Foreign policy must rest on each nation’s enlightened determination of its own sovereigninterests. It is a considered judgment, drawn from a nation’s history, its values and the commitments it has freely made to others. It must be guided by principle, not expediency.

If ever Cuba needed our support, it is now. Our Caribbean neighbour faces the threat of extinction from a hegemon that denies energy, food, medicine, water and sanitation to human beings whose only sin is to be Cuban.

International law cannot be selectively applied. Inhumane measures of this kind are not imposed upon great powers whose political systems differ from that of the United States. They are imposed upon Cuba because Cuba is small and adjacent. Jamaica cannot afford to look away.

The Government speaks of encouraging dialogue between Washington and Havana and reform within Cuba, and the Minister reminds us that the Prime Minister raised these matters with his CARICOM colleagues in St Kitts and Nevis. If dialogue between Washington and Havana is indeed the Government’s objective, the Jamaican people are entitled to know what initiatives have been taken since the St Kitts and Nevis meeting, and what role CARICOM has been invited to play. Absent such an account, the language of dialogue cannot justify a drastic change of policy.

The people of Cuba stood with us whenever we needed support, and asked nothing in return. Their doctors and nurses served in our rural clinics and hospitals. Through Operation Miracle, nearly 25,000 Jamaicans have had their sight restored or improved, free of charge. Cuba’s scholarships trained our young people. Cuba donated and built schools that have benefited generations of teachers and students. That solidarity was freely given.

And how have we repaid it? By sending the Cuban doctors and nurses home, terminating a medical cooperation programme that had served our people for half a century. By concluding an arrangement to receive from the United States deportees who have no connection to Jamaica, the so-called third-country nationals (TCN) deal, entered into without consultation with Parliament or the people, and still kept secret. And now, by this abstention.

Nor is Cuba the only cause on which this Government has lost its voice. Last year, on a crucial vote pertaining to Palestine and its people, Jamaica chose to be absent from the chamber. That was not neutrality. It was cowardice. One hundred and forty-five countries voted in favour. 

Taken together, these egregious errors form a pattern: absence from the vote in support of the Palestinian people; the sending home of the Cubans; the secret TCN deal; and now the UN vote on Cuba. Each step has been taken quietly; each has been explained away; and each carries Jamaica further from the principled ground on which we have always stood.

Jamaica has a long and honourable record in the councils of the world. That record was not built by abstaining when principle was on the line. It was built by a small nation that proved, time and again, what it means to say: we likkle but we tallawah. On apartheid, and in the struggles of the developing world for a just international order, our voice carried a weight far beyond our size, because the world knew we could not be bought or bent. We are now in mortal danger of losing the universal respect we once enjoyed, and respect squandered is not easily regained.

The harm is not confined to our internal reputation and standing abroad. It is felt in every Jamaican household, at home and across the Diaspora. Jamaicans in Toronto and London, in New York and Miami, who have carried our name with pride and defended our nation wherever they have gone, are offended, hurt, angry and ashamed that their Government has chosen to shatter our nation’s reputation in this way. They did not help to build that reputation so that it could be traded away in a single vote.

The entire nation and the Diaspora are entitled to a full and truthful account of how this decision was taken, by whom, and on whose advice. They are entitled to know whether pressure was applied, from what quarter, and what, if anything, was promised or threatened. They are entitled to a Parliament whose unanimous resolutions are honoured, not set aside overnight in New York. And they are entitled to see Jamaica restored to the position which successive Administrations of both parties have proudly held.

We are a people who came through the holds of slave ships, the brutality of the plantation and the long humiliation of colonial rule. We did not win our freedom in order to bend the knee. Our good name was earned after centuries of profound oppression, and a proud people is rightly jealous of it.

Those who lead such a people act in its name. They must never mortgage its good name for favour, nor trade its principles for the promise of reward or the avoidance of displeasure. They must never mistake silence for prudence, or submission for statecraft. What they must do is speak, as Jamaica has always spoken, for the right of the small to stand unafraid before the strong.

The time has come to repudiate, once and for all, the habits of genuflection. We live in no one’s backyard. Jamaica must never accept the doctrine that might makes right.

When the annals of this era are written, they willrecord that on 28 October 2026 a Government of Jamaica resiled from our finest traditions of standing for law, justice, and sovereign equality but that the people of Jamaica did not.

news.title: Rubio says US not directly involved in Flavio Bolsonaro’s flight from Brazil
news.text:
ATLANTA: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that Washington was not directly involved in Flavio Bolsonaro’s arrangements to leave Brazil after his election loss.

President Donald Trump said that Bolsonaro could, however, stay in the United States “as long as he wants.”

Bolsonaro, who lost his bid to be president in Sunday’s run-off vote, arrived with his family in the US on Wednesday after a court ordered his passports to be seized amid multiple investigations against him.

“He had previously held a visa, and the president made a decision to allow him to enter the country,” Rubio told a press conference in Atlanta, Georgia, where he hosted G20 foreign ministers for a two-day meeting.

Rubio added that “the US government was not involved directly” in arrangements Bolsonaro made to leave his country.

Following the vote, the 45-year-old bolted from Brazil via Argentina and Ecuador in a plane that some US media, including The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal, reported was chartered by Jason Miller, an adviser to Trump.

The plane that whisked the Bolsonaro family to the US was paid for by an intermediary from a US bank account, the head of the airline has told AFP.

The White House has not commented on the flight, but Trump has called the Brazilian election “disgraceful.”

Speaking to reporters at his Florida residence on Saturday, Trump said he had no plans to meet Bolsonaro but voiced sympathy for the rightist senator.

“I think he got treated very shabbily. Very shabbily, so he can stay here as long as he wants,” the president said.

A Brazilian diplomatic source, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that Argentina’s diplomatic representative had been summoned for a “routine meeting” to “provide explanations” on the flight.

Argentina’s foreign minister later denied that Brazil had asked Buenos Aires to explain its role in the operation.

Since arriving in the US, Bolsonaro has claimed to be the true leader of Brazil and said that he left the country because he was a victim of “persecution.”

Flavio Bolsonaro’s father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for plotting a coup after his 2022 re-election loss.
news.summary: Marco Rubio stated the US was not directly involved in Flavio Bolsonaro’s departure from Brazil post-election. Trump expressed that Bolsonaro could remain in the US indefinitely.

news.title: List of Trump's Media Lawsuits as Judge Tosses WSJ Epstein Note Case
news.text: A federal judge dismissed President Donald Trump's defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal, delivering the latest setback in his broader legal campaign against major U.S. news organizations. In an order issued Saturday, U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed Trump's suit against the newspaper, its parent companies and two reporters with prejudice, meaning the claims cannot be refiled in their current form. The lawsuit stemmed from a July 2025 Journal article reporting on a purported birthday letter sent to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Trump denied authoring the letter and sued the newspaper, alleging defamation. Gayles ruled that Trump failed, for a second time, to plausibly allege that the defendants acted with "actual malice," the constitutional standard public figures must meet to prevail in defamation cases. The judge repeatedly cited the landmark Supreme Court decision New York Times v. Sullivan, which established heightened protections for press coverage of public officials. "The costs and efforts required to defend a lawsuit ... could chill free speech nearly as effectively as the absence of the actual malice standard altogether," Gayles wrote while explaining why public figures must plausibly allege actual malice at the outset of litigation. The court also rejected Trump's argument that the Journal acted recklessly by publishing the article after he denied its central claim. "In effect, President Trump argues that once he declared the Letter a 'fake,' Defendants should have disregarded everything else they learned in their investigation and not published the story," Gayles wrote. "But that is not what the actual malice standard requires." The ruling marks one of the most significant court defeats yet for Trump's recent efforts to use defamation litigation against major media outlets. Pending: Trump's $10B Lawsuit Against BBC Trump is suing the BBC in a federal court in Miami regarding a Panorama documentary that spliced together portions of Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech. The suit seeks $5 billion in damages for each of the two counts listed—one count of defamation and one count of violating a Florida trade practices law. While the BBC apologized for the edit, the outlet denies defamation. "As we have made clear previously, we will be defending this case," a BBC spokesperson said in December 2025. Trump has been ordered to sit for a deposition by December 11, and the judge warned Trump this week that the case could be dismissed if he does not produce more relevant documents or evidence showing his legal team's search for them. Pending: CNN, MS NOW and Politico Lawsuit Three media outlets filed a First Amendment lawsuit in September after Trump banned them from the White House and escorted reporters off the White Houst grounds. CNN, MS NOW and Politico argued that the ban was retaliation for unfavorable coverage and violated the First Amendment and due-process protections. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Trump, granted a temporary restraining order on September 24 and ordered the White House to restore the outlets' credentials. He said they were likely to succeed on their claim that the administration revoked access without adequate standards or due process. He converted the order to a preliminary injunction on October 14 to keep the outlets in the White House while the case proceeds. He found they were likely to prevail on both First Amendment and due-process claims. Kelly wrote that Trump's own statements suggested the ban was motivated by displeasure with the outlets' coverage, making it likely unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination. The outlets amended their complaint on October 28 to argue that even though White House credentials were restored, the Trump administration was excluding them from pool assignments in the Oval Office and on Air Force One. They are asking the court to restore that access as well. Pending: Trump's $15B Lawsuit Against the New York Times Trump sought $15 billion in damages from The New York Times, several of its reporters and Penguin Random House over reporting and the book Lucky Loser: How Donald Trump Squandered His Father's Fortune and Created the Illusion of Success. A federal judge dismissed the defamation lawsuit in September 2025. U.S. District Judge Steven Merryday, appointed by Republican President George H.W. Bush, said Trump's filing violated rules requiring a clear and concise explanation for relief, adding that a lawsuit is not "a public forum for vituperation and invective" or "a protected platform to rage against an adversary." "A complaint is not a megaphone for public relations or a podium for a passionate oration at a political rally or the functional equivalent of the Hyde Park Speakers' Corner," Merryday wrote. Rather than ending the case, however, Merryday allowed Trump to file an amended complaint. Trump later submitted a revised version, and the litigation remains pending. Pending: Trump's $1B Lawsuit Against Pulitzer Board Trump is seeking at least $1 billion in damages from members of the Pulitzer Prize Board over a 2022 statement defending the Pulitzer Prizes awarded to The New York Times and The Washington Post for reporting on Russian interference in the 2016 election. Trump argues the statement was defamatory. The case has survived dismissal efforts and remains active in Florida, where discovery and pretrial proceedings are continuing. In December 2025, the Pulitzer Prize Board asked a Florida court to compel Trump to hand over his tax returns, financial records, and full medical and psychological files in a sweeping discovery request aimed at testing his claims of reputational and emotional harm. A spokesperson for the Pulitzer Board told Newsweek: “Just like any other plaintiff, the president must articulate and prove his claims with evidence." In August, the judge in the case was removed after the Freedom of the Press Foundation filed a complaint alleging that the judge who ruled that Trump's case could proceed was being considered for a federal appointment. Settled: Trump's $10B Lawsuit Over CBS Interview The president and Paramount Global settled a lawsuit over CBS News' 60 Minutes interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris in October 2024 for $16 million. Trump argued that the interview with Harris, who was Trump’s Democratic opponent in that year's presidential election, had been edited to her benefit. The lawsuit challenges "CBS' partisan and unlawful acts of election and voter interference through malicious, deceptive, and substantial news distortion calculated to confuse, deceive, and mislead the public," according to court documents. Trump's attorneys argued that Bill Whitaker's interview with Harris was edited to "attempt to tip the scales in favor of the Democratic Party as the heated 2024 Presidential Election—which President Trump is leading—approaches its conclusion." The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, sought $10 billion in damages. Settled: Trump's Lawsuit Against ABC News In a deal announced on December 14, 2024, ABC News agreed to pay $15 million toward Trump's presidential library and issue a public apology to settle a defamation lawsuit over inaccurate statements made by anchor George Stephanopoulos during a broadcast earlier this year. The lawsuit was filed after Stephanopoulos said during a March 10 segment of ABC News' This Week while interviewing Representative Nancy Mace, a South Carolina Republican, that Trump had been "found liable for rape." While Trump was found liable for sexually abusing and defaming writer E. Jean Carroll, neither verdict involved a finding of rape as defined under New York law. In his lawsuit, Trump had accused Stephanopoulos of acting with "actual malice." Dismissed: Trump's Lawsuit Over Iowa Poll Trump sued The Des Moines Register, Gannett and veteran pollster J. Ann Selzer over a final 2024 Iowa poll that showed then-Vice President Harris leading in the state before Trump ultimately won it. The lawsuit sought substantial damages and alleged the poll was deceptive and amounted to election interference. An Iowa judge dismissed the case in September, finding the poll and related reporting were protected speech. In a written ruling on Wednesday, Judge Scott Beattie of Iowa’s Fifth Judicial District dismissed the lawsuit filed by Trump, Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, and former Iowa State Senator Brad Zaun. The suit was dismissed with prejudice, which means Trump cannot file the same claim again. A spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said at the time that the president plans to appeal to the Iowa Supreme Court, vowing to pursue “a just and winning conclusion.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story.
news.summary: The ruling marks one of the most significant court defeats yet for Trump's efforts to use defamation litigation against the media.
news.author: Jennifer Radcliffe

news.title: Indian American lawmaker hits back after Trump calls him ‘lightweight, total dope’
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 1 (IANS) Indian American Congressman Ro Khanna has hit back at President Donald Trump, who attacked him repeatedly on Friday over his criticism of the cost of the war with Iran, calling him a “lightweight” at the White House and a “total dope” at a campaign rally in Florida. Speaking in the Oval Office on October 30, Trump said: “I watch this guy, Ro Khanna, who’s a lightweight. And he was saying that, ‘President Trump is spending a lot of money.’ Well, I spent a lot of money in order to get rid of a nuclear weapon, which we’ve done.” “But any money we’ve spent in Iran, we’ve more than made up for with what we did in Venezuela, taken in hundreds of billions of dollars, many, many times,” Trump said. Later in the day, at a midterm rally in Daytona, Florida, Trump returned to the Democratic lawmaker from California. “I watch this total dope, Ro Khanna,” Trump said, according to HuffPost. “Fox puts him on all the time. You know, Fox is giving Democrats more time than they give Republicans.” “I’m working my ass off, I’m doing rallies -- and I come back and I watch the opponent of the person I did the rally for. I’m not happy. But I watched Ro Khanna, of course, on Fox this morning. I can’t watch him,” Trump said. Trump also called Khanna a “radical left loser” over his calls for impeachment. Khanna responded on X. “Thanks for the 4 shoutouts today, Mr. President. I’ll be on Fox this Sunday to share more of my thoughts on your failure in Iran and how it’s raised gas and food prices,” he wrote. “If you get a break from bragging about oil company profits and playing golf, tune in!” he added. He did not say which Fox programme he would appear on. In an earlier post, Khanna wrote: “Trump said Bush ‘didn’t seem smart’ for spending trillions in the Middle East. Now he calls me a ‘lightweight’ for opposing $47B in Iran.” “Spend that money on jobs and childcare for Americans. His voters wanted him to stay out of war. He lied. Result: Blue Tsunami Tuesday,” Khanna wrote. The $47 billion figure is Khanna’s. HuffPost described it as the estimated cost of the war. Khanna had appeared on “Fox & Friends” hours before Trump’s remarks, criticising the Iran war and raising possible impeachment proceedings. Khanna, who represents California’s 17th Congressional District in Silicon Valley, is among the most prominent Indian American members of Congress and a frequent critic of the administration’s foreign policy. Americans vote in the midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3.

news.title: US Judge Dismisses Trump Lawsuit Against Wall Street Journal over Epstein Letter
news.text: WASHINGTON: A US judge on Saturday dismissed President Donald Trump's defamation lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and media magnate Rupert Murdoch over a report that Trump sent a bawdy birthday letter to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Trump had sued for $10 billion after the newspaper's story was published in July 2025 detailing the president's alleged 2003 letter to Epstein, which apparently featured a drawing of a naked woman. Murdoch is the founder of News Corp. which owns the Wall Street Journal. The report piled scrutiny on Trump from both Democrats and his own Republican party, who rejected the president's attempts to downplay the saga as a hoax and called for a full release of legal files on Epstein. In Saturday's ruling, Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed Trump's lawsuit with prejudice, meaning Trump cannot file an amended version of the suit, as he did when Gayles turned down an initial version of it back in April. The judge wrote that in bringing his defamation claim, Trump had both times failed to establish that the defendants "acted with actual malice." The House Oversight Committee last year published a copy of Trump's alleged birthday note to Epstein, which consists of a short dialogue between "Donald" and "Jeffrey." "We have certain things in common," says Donald, to which Jeffrey responds: "Yes, we do, come to think of it." "Enigmas never age, have you noticed that?" asks Donald. "As a matter of fact, it was clear to me the last time I saw you," says Jeffrey. "A pal is a wonderful thing. Happy Birthday -- and may every day be another wonderful secret," the note ends, followed by Trump's signature, which takes the place of pubic hair on the nude outline. - Epstein files - Trump's supporters have been obsessed with the Epstein case for years and held as an article of faith that "deep state" elites were protecting a sex ring of Epstein associates, particularly in the Democratic Party and Hollywood. The president fought for months to prevent the Department of Justice from releasing the so-called "Epstein Files" but eventually signed a law passed by Congress requiring their publication. Trump's name appears repeatedly in the documents but he denies any wrongdoing and has not been charged with any criminal offenses connected to the affair. High-profile figures including Britain's former prince Andrew have been publicly disgraced for their associations with Epstein. Ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections which will decide control of Congress, Democrats have reportedly spent more than $35 million on Epstein-related advertisements. With a Republican majority in the House and Senate, Trump has so far enjoyed relatively little political opposition since taking office in January 2025, giving the courts a key role in limiting him. In a separate case Saturday, a new suit was filed to prevent Trump's attempt to erect a huge triumphal arch in front of the iconic military cemetery outside Washington. That is one of a number of projects launched by Trump in a bid to put his personal stamp on the capital, including a ballroom at the White House and a laborious renovation of the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall. On Friday, a US federal judge pushed back on government assertions that the planned arch -- which Trump has said would house drones and snipers -- was needed for national security. "It's something (the) region needs militarily and I think aesthetically also," Trump told reporters late Saturday. "We're going to see if we can get it built."

news.title: They wanted Karen Bass to resign after the fire — now they’re voting for her
news.text:
Many residents of Pacific Palisades wanted Karen Bass to resign after the fire in January 2025. Now they will vote to re-elect her as mayor of LA.

It’s not because she’s done a much better job since then. It’s because Nithya Raman is a socialist with radical ideas and extremist supporters. 

After the pandemic, the riots, and the fire, the last thing residents want is more upheaval. 

Rebuilding lives, and homes, is difficult enough as it is. What people want most is stability.

Before the fire, most of LA’s problems didn’t reach Pacific Palisades.

Residents tried to keep the city’s failures at arm’s length. Until the fire brought them home.

Many residents supported Spencer Pratt for mayor in the primary election.

They were — and remain — furious about all of the government failures in the fire.

Karen Bass wasn’t even in LA. She was in Ghana, on a mission for the outgoing Biden administration.

Ironically, President Joe Biden was in LA. The reason Pacific Palisades had no police directing evacuations during the fire was that they were protecting the president.

The city and state also failed to position firefighters where they were needed.

So residents were on their own.

Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters 

People fought the fire with garden hoses, until the water ran out. 

The reservoir was empty, which was inexcusable. 

But even if it had been full, the water system would have lost pressure due to the sudden demand. The system wasn’t designed for wildfires. 

That wasn’t Karen Bass’ fault. But plenty of things were.

In the aftermath, she seemed to have no idea what to do. It was only after President Donald Trump visited, and publicly argued with the mayor, that she allowed residents to visit their burned homes.

As people sifted through the ruins, and fought with their insurance companies, they wondered if rebuilding was worth the risk.

Many wanted to come back to Pacific Palisades, but they wanted a commitment from the city that nothing like the fire could ever happen again.

Spencer Pratt channeled that desire for change. Not everyone liked his style. But at least he was offering common-sense solutions to the city’s problems.

As for Raman, she was invisible in Pacific Palisades after the fire. Her campaign staff will claim that she visited — and she did, once she was running for mayor.

But she’s also a socialist. And the deepest fear many residents had in Pacific Palisades is that the rest of the city would refuse to help — that people would see the place as a bunch of rich white people on the hill and leave residents to fend for themselves.

Some also feared that the city would try to seize land for low-income housing in Pacific Palisades, which is exactly what Raman’s socialist party manifesto says it wants to do, in general.

Raman seemed like a fringe candidate. She had trouble explaining to reporters why she was running. And Pratt ran circles around her and Bass in their primary debate.

So it was a shock to many in Pacific Palisades when Raman finished ahead of Pratt and qualified for the general election.

After that, many residents gave up on changing the city, politically. The focus has shifted to what they can do for themselves.

They just want the politicians to stay out of the way. And Karen Bass has been good at that.

Raman and her staff are — like Zohran Mamdani’s team in New York — bright, confident, and determined. 

They also seem to have no idea why socialism has never worked. But they’re going to try.

The Pacific Palisades wants no part of it.

The local Jewish community is also wary of Raman.

Her socialists have targeted Jewish houses of worship and schools with anti-Israel protests.

It’s noteworthy that their manifesto singles out a Jewish security group for de-funding.

Raman told a Jewish community forum in September that she believed Israel had committed “genocide” in Gaza.

That is plainly untrue. And it is also the pretext that radical protesters have used when targeting Jewish institutions in LA.

At the community forum, Raman also defended appearing on a podcast with antisemite Hasan Piker. She also said she would appear on other podcasts hosted by hateful people, as long as they had an audience to reach. 

Why would any mayor of LA want to reach an audience of bigots?

Some of the Jewish residents of Pacific Palisades were prepared to give Raman a chance before that forum. 

Not anymore.

news.title: Epstein letter row: Judge rejects Trump's $10 billion defamation suit against WSJ
news.text: A federal judge in the United States on Saturday dismissed president Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal for the second time this year. The court ruled that Trump had failed to establish that the newspaper acted with “actual malice” in its reporting on an alleged birthday letter bearing his name and linked to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.US district Judge Darrin P Gayles, sitting in Miami, dismissed the lawsuit with prejudice, meaning Trump cannot refile the same case. Describing the president’s arguments as “grasping at straws”, the judge said the amended complaint failed to meet the legal threshold for establishing defamation.According to the Associated Press (AP), this is the second time Gayles has dismissed Trump's lawsuit this year. The judge first threw out the case in April, ruling that Trump had failed to sufficiently argue that the newspaper published the report with actual malice. However, Gayles allowed the president to file an amended complaint, which was submitted in May. The revised lawsuit has now also been dismissed.“The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice,” Gayles wrote.“Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false,” he added.The lawsuit arose from a Wall Street Journal report published last year about a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the newspaper said bore Trump's name. The material was reportedly included in an album compiled for Epstein's 50th birthday in 2003.According to the newspaper, the letter was collected by British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell. It contained text framed by the outline of what appeared to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ended with the words: “Happy Birthday -- and may every day be another wonderful secret.”Trump denied writing the letter and described the report as “false, malicious, and defamatory”.His lawsuit accused Dow Jones, the newspaper's parent company, Rupert Murdoch and other defendants of having “knowingly and recklessly” published “numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements”. It also alleged “overwhelming financial and reputational harm” and sought $10 billion in damages.Gayles rejected the argument that the newspaper should have withheld its report following Trump's denial.“Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it,” the judge wrote.In his ruling, Gayles cited the US Supreme Court's 1964 judgment in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, which requires public figures to establish that a publication knowingly made false statements or acted with reckless disregard for the truth.The dismissal comes amid Trump's wider legal confrontations with media organisations, including disputes involving the BBC and The Associated Press.  Custos Fuller installed as Mico University College chancellor 







Custos of Kingston, Steadman Fuller, was on Thursday installed as the third Chancellor of The Mico University College.

It was a full circle moment for the chairman and managing director of Kingston Bookshop Limited, who completed his teacher training at the institution 53 years ago.

He taught briefly at Water Valley All Age School in St Mary before embarking on a career in business and public service, making significant contributions to Jamaica’s book industry, literacy and intellectual development.

Addressing the installation ceremony held at King’s House, Governor-General Sir Patrick Allen said Custos Fuller’s appointment is a fitting recognition of his achievements, service, and continuing contribution to Jamaica.

“His excellent service as Custos Rotolorum for the Parish of Kingston, his wider responsibilities in national life and the many times he deputised as Governor-General, when I’m unavailable, these experiences speak to a record of service, leadership and public trust,” he said.

He noted that despite leaving the classroom, Custos Fuller has continued his dedication to education through the Kingston Bookshop, sourcing textbooks from the United Kingdom and other countries to support schools, educators, and students across Jamaica and the wider Caribbean.

“He has demonstrated that nation building takes many forms and that entrepreneurship, when guided by vision and purpose, can become a powerful instrument of educational advancement,” he stated.

The governor-general commended Custos Fuller’s enduring relationship with his alma mater, noting that his service on Mico’s board and committees reflects a sustained commitment to the institution that helped shape him today.

“When we were public school teachers at Water Valley All Age School, little could we have imagined the remarkable journeys that laid ahead of us and that we would one day reunite in these distinguished circumstances,” he said.

“May your tenure as Chancellor be fruitful and purposeful and may your leadership further strengthen Mico’s enduring mission of preparing generations to teach, to lead and to serve guided by its motto, ‘Do It With Thy Might’,” the governor-general expressed.

Education, Skills, Youth and Information Minister, Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon, congratulated Custos Fuller, describing him as a distinguished Jamaican whose life exemplifies service.

“You assume this office at an important time in Jamaica’s development and at a defining moment in the history of this distinguished institution. I am confident that your experience, your wisdom, your commitment to service and your deep connection to Mico will contribute meaningfully to its continued growth and success. I pray that your tenure will be marked by innovation, strong partnerships, institutional advancement and most importantly, an unwavering commitment to the development of Jamaica’s educators and our young people,” she said.

President, Mico University College, Dr Asburn Pinnock, said the institution looks forward to Custos Fuller’s leadership, counsel and support as it strengthens institutional capacity, expand opportunities to students, and advance teacher education and research and deepen contribution to national and regional development.

He noted that his appointment presents an important chapter in the continuing story of The Mico University College.

“It represents the heritage, values, and aspirations of our institution and provides an important link between its historic foundation and the future ambition.

As you assume this office, you do so at a time when education is being reshaped by technological advancement, changing social expectations, economic uncertainty, and a growing demand for innovation and the resurgence of excellence,” he stated.

“We welcome you home, the man of 1973 and a Bucks Knight, and look forward to working with you and advancing the institutional mission and aspiration,” he said.

President Pinnock saluted outgoing Chancellor, Dr Roderick James, and the institution’s first chancellor, Professor Errol Miller.

Chancellor Fuller, in his response, gave his commitment to strengthening Mico’s capacity to shape Jamaica, improving research, embracing innovation, attracting excellent students, and continuing to serve children and communities.

news.title: Trump flags Iran targets as talks continue
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 1 (IANS) US President Donald Trump on Saturday named Pickaxe Mountain as an Iranian site that needed to be dealt with, while saying negotiations with Tehran were progressing and leaving open whether diplomacy would produce an agreement. Speaking to reporters in Palm Beach, Florida, Trump said there were still one or two sites to address. His remarks came hours after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the president had not decided whether to launch fresh military action against Iran. “You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that,” Trump said. The president described the Iran negotiations as “going fine”, but questioned Tehran’s reliability. “We'll see if they make a deal,” he said. Trump also suggested that dealing with the remaining sites could be accomplished rapidly. Earlier in Atlanta, Rubio declined to discuss possible military operations or say how long diplomatic efforts would be given to succeed. He said decisions on timing rested with Trump. “We can achieve military objectives if we seek to. He hasn’t made a decision. I have no announcement in that regard with you today, and nor do we take any of it lightly,” Rubio told reporters at the conclusion of the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting. Rubio said Trump preferred a diplomatic outcome and would already have acted if military force had been his preferred course. “He’d prefer to solve it diplomatically,” he said. Asked about Qatari-backed talks, Rubio said contacts with Iran had continued through several channels, including intermediaries and, in some cases, direct conversations. He declined to assess their progress or specify a deadline. “There are multiple talks; talks have actually never stopped,” he said. Rubio said Washington remained open to a diplomatic solution, but any arrangement would have to address US security concerns. He identified preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons and confronting its support for armed groups across the Middle East as central American objectives. The secretary also linked the confrontation to commercial shipping, accusing Iran of targeting vessels carrying energy supplies and other cargo. He specifically referred to ships with Indian sailors aboard. Those allegations were made by Rubio during the press conference. The material reviewed for this report did not include an Iranian response. Rubio said US forces were defending shipping against drones and missiles and called for wider international participation in protecting passage through the Strait of Hormuz. He described cooperation from other countries as limited and said the burden had fallen primarily on the United States. The Atlanta meeting formed part of preparations for the G20 leaders’ summit in Florida in December. Its agenda included energy, supply chains, critical minerals, food security and freedom of navigation, reflecting the economic consequences of disruptions to international commerce. Maritime security was a recurring subject in the discussions. Rubio said interruptions to the movement of energy, fertiliser and agricultural products threatened food supplies, while acknowledging that participants agreed more readily on the problems than on collective solutions.

news.title: Trump Melts Down at Reporter at Tacky Mar-a-Lago Halloween Party
news.text:
President Donald Trump has once again mocked a journalist for asking a question he didn’t approve of. 

Holding a press gaggle in the middle of his Mar-a-Lago jungle-themed Halloween party, Trump took questions surrounded by blue-suited Secret Service members and at least one person dressed as what appeared to be a parrot. 

“Do you expect to go back to war with Iran this week,” a journalist asked. 

After having to get part of the question repeated, Trump, 80, snapped. 

“Why would you ask such a stupid question?” he began, then referencing that the reporter was from the New York Times.

“New York Times. OK, Let’s say I did, would I tell you?”

Then Trump adopted a mocking expression and repeated the question he had been asked, mimicking the journalist. 

“Would I tell you? Let’s say I did, would I tell you?” he repeated. “It’s not a question for the New York Times. 

Without attempting any kind of genuine answer to the question, Trump then changed the subject. 

There has been much speculation that aggression against Iran will pick up once the midterms are over, as the war is highly unpopular. A White House official told MS NOW that, “we do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist. President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon.”

The president’s relationship with the media has almost always been fraught, but in recent months it has deteriorated significantly. 

He banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House and also excluded CNN from Air Force One when the network was supposed to be covering the president for all the networks. 

Earlier this week he insulted a journalist’s weight when he asked Trump a question about his health, and he has repeatedly targeted female journalists with comments about their appearance. 

The Halloween briefing was a quick 11 minute back-and-forth in a room packed with people, and Trump was keen to show off his party. 

“These are the biggest guys on Wall Street and they spent all day long getting ready, I only had 10 minutes,” he lamented, before complaining he was only going to have “15 minutes of Halloween” before returning to work.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“Anybody that can do what he did in politics and get resounding results, and not only that, he has the safest county in the United States of America [according to US News & World Report] … He’s a great manager.”

Despite recent polls showing Hochul ahead anywhere from 11 to 14 points, Trump said he expects the Nassau County executive to win.

“I’ll be waiting for his call,” the president said. “I bet he’s going to be one of the first calls if he wins, and he’ll get tremendous help from the federal government. And it’s hard to help people that do such a bad job. It’s almost like throwing good money after bad.”

Hochul spokesperson Ryan Radulovack responded by attempting to paint Trump as a boogeyman, something the governor has also done many times throughout the campaign.

“Blakeman … started with the promise to ‘bring Trump-style leadership to Albany,’ and his closing message is telling people how little he regrets going full Trump in this campaign,” added Radulovack. 

“Gov. Hochul has put money back in New Yorkers’ pockets, invested $4 billion in public safety, and fought back against Trump’s attacks,” while Blakeman “defends everything Trump does.”

Trump during the tele-rally also found some time to claim that the war with Iran is all but over.

“We’re winning very easily the war with Iran,” Trump said. 

“They’re talking to us. They’re negotiating, but they do a lot of talking. And we’ll see what happens.”

“But one way or the other, their Navy’s gone. Their Air Force is gone. All blown up. All at the bottom of the sea, and they’re not going to have a nuclear weapon. It’s very simple, and they know that. They know that, and we can end it any time we want.”

At the Atlanta press conference, Rubio described Washington’s immediate priority as seeking a negotiated end to the Russia-Ukraine war. He said the United States remained engaged because it communicated with both sides and was being encouraged by other countries to continue its efforts. He pointed to attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, civilian deaths and the long-term task of rebuilding the country’s economy and electricity network. Rubio also warned about the possibility of the conflict spreading, citing sabotage and drones entering NATO countries’ airspace. “There’s a lot of danger involved in that as well,” he said. Any agreement on shipping would address some of the war’s international consequences without settling the underlying conflict. “We’d like to see it happen. It doesn’t solve the war problem, but at least it diminishes some of the impact – spillover impact that it’s having on the food security of vulnerable countries,” he said. The G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta was part of preparations for the leaders’ summit in Doral, Florida, in December. news.title: Over 40% of names on DOJ list of alleged noncitizens are not on California voter rolls, analysis finds
news.text:
ReutersA recent analysis by UCLA found that over 40% of names flagged as noncitizen voters in California are absent from voter rolls

Washington: More than 4 in 10 names flagged as possible noncitizen voters in California by the Trump administration cannot be found on the state's voter rolls, according to a legal filing Saturday by an immigrant-rights group.It's the first outside analysis of a list that the Department of Justice has used to threaten prosecution of election officials. The analysis also found that thousands of U.S. citizens appear to be flagged as ineligible to vote on the government's list.The contention was made in a filing by two data analysts at the University of California, Los Angeles. They analyzed the 20,930 names that the department demanded that California election officials treat as possible illegal voters by separating their ballots during the vote count on Election Day.Multiple judges have rejected the demand as unconstitutional and a threat to democracy, and local and state officials have said the list appears riddled with errors.Court filing outlines problems with government listThe breadth of the problems with the list was outlined in Saturday's filing. It describes an analysis by two members of UCLA's Voting Rights Project, who filed a lawsuit challenging it with the Los Angeles-based Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, or CHIRLA.Live EventsThe research found that 8,880 of the names, representing 42% of the entire list, do not correspond to anyone in California's current voter file. It also found at least 22 are U.S. citizens, and many more may correspond to those of confirmed citizens."The expert analysis further makes clear that the mandated voter list endangers a significant number of eligible California voter," said the filing, which was cosigned by Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for California governor and an adviser to the UCLA Voting Rights Project.The Trump administration had objected to sharing the list, calling it a "fishing expedition" and noting that it included sensitive information. On Saturday, the federal prosecutor who spearheaded the Trump case in California called the analysis "bogus.""This is a bogus report by the activist illegal immigrant rights group CHIRLA," Bill Essayli, who runs the U.S. Attorney's office in Los Angeles, posted on X.Also on Saturday, President Donald Trump bemoaned the legal rulings against his effort to force California to separate votes from the individuals his administration labels suspected noncitizens, even though one came from a judge he himself nominated.In a social media post, Trump claimed his Justice Department found "20,000, but potentially Hundreds of Thousands, and maybe even Millions," of fraudulent votes, "and the Court has just ruled against it. Why would they reject fixing Election Fraud?"The Trump administration has also urged Washington state to remove what it says were 400 possible noncitizens on its rolls, though state election officials there say that list is also unreliable and includes one voter who cast ballots in the 1990s.The Justice Department has warned California election officials they could face criminal liability if they let noncitizens vote and issued subpoenas of election offices there.Election officials say they have no time to investigateElection officials have complained that the Trump administration has confronted them with lists of possible illegal voters at the last minute before Election Day, with no time to conduct the painstaking investigation required by law before removing someone from the rolls.Multiple lawsuits have been filed to stop the administration from continuing to threaten local election officials.On Friday, a federal judge in California ordered the Justice Department to stop sending demands to state officials, a decision the Trump administration appealed Saturday. Several counties in the state had run quick checks of the Trump list and found numerous errors.Saturday's broader analysis was possible because a federal judge on Friday ordered the Trump administration to share the list with the plaintiffs in the case.CHIRLA and the UCLA project sued the Homeland Security Department in early October to prevent it from using federal immigration data to challenge state voter rolls. The lawsuit cited examples in other states where the federal government's data has been proven to mistakenly include thousands of citizens.Case argues that government's methods pose risk to votingThe case argued that the data-matching methods risk disenfranchising or deterring citizens from voting. On top of that, plaintiffs argued, the lists could disproportionately target naturalized citizens who are legally entitled to vote.Applying the government's methodology, the UCLA researchers found that nearly 7,500 naturalized citizens in the state were "highly likely" to be incorrectly flagged as ineligible.The researchers noted that the administration apparently removed the voter identification number from the names, making it harder for election officials to determine whether the flagged individuals were already on their rolls or were duplicates in the Justice Department list. They described the voter ID number as the most crucial data point.The Justice Department argues that there is just as much to lose if the ballots aren't separated."Every ballot cast by an ineligible voter cancels out the vote of an American citizen," Kiersten V. Pels, a spokesperson for the department, wrote in an email. "The Department makes no apology for protecting those votes."Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Virginia and DC sue over Trump's arch, adding to legal challenges as government wants work to begin
news.text: WASHINGTON — The legal challenges to President Donald Trump's proposed memorial arch are mounting, with the District of Columbia and Virginia suing in federal court Saturday as the administration says construction could begin as early as next week.U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan proceeded to consolidate that lawsuit with the original one she is overseeing and ordered a joint briefing schedule for the lawsuits.All the plaintiffs are calling for a halt to potential work on a monument that would rise 250 feet (76 meters) on a patch of grass off the bridge that spans the Potomac River, connecting the city with Arlington National Cemetery. That would make the arch 100 feet taller (30 meters) than the Statue of Liberty is from its base to the top of the torch.Chutkan is already considering issuing an order to halt the project until the original lawsuit against the Trump administration by three Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian is resolved. She held a hearing Friday but did not immediately act, though she said she would move expeditiously.In the latest filing, two attorneys general, Brian Schwalb of Washington and Jay Jones of Virginia, argue that 'as soon as Defendants break ground on this project, they will inflict irreparable harm on both the District and Virginia. The Arch site sits at the center of a major traffic artery between the District and Virginia, in the monumental core of the capital, on an island that straddles the Potomac River. During the three-year period of construction, the Arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges.'As the original plaintiffs have, they also are seeking a temporary restraining order that would slow the administration's plans to move ahead imminently with construction.'The Triumphal Arch in Memorial Circle is going to be one of the most iconic landmarks not only in Washington, D.C., but throughout the world,' said White House spokesman Davis Ingle in an email. 'It will serve as a gateway to Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen, and all Americans alike, serving as a visual reminder of the noble sacrifices borne by so many American heroes throughout our 250 year history so we can enjoy our freedoms today.'The lawsuit raises concerns about how the traffic interruption would impact emergency responses in a region where joint operations are the norm, including the January 2025 midair collision between a military helicopter and airliner that killed 67.Administration wants to get started on constructionSpeaking to reporters during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Saturday night, Trump said the arch 'is very important militarily for Washington, D.C., and our country. It's also going to be the most beautiful arc ever built.''It will be one of Washington's most beautiful things. It's also very important militarily. Maybe more importantly, but I don't think so,' Trump added. 'But it is very important militarily, and I think we're doing very well.'He said 'whether it's Virginia, Maryland, or Washington — it doesn't matter. It's something the region needs militarily, and I think aesthetically also.'Trump's administration, in a recent court filing, said it had plans to seek final approval of the project, a Trump favorite, at Thursday's meeting of the National Capital Planning Commission and possibly begin construction the same day, despite the then-two active lawsuits pending.On Friday, the government submitted a 106-page plan for the arch that envisions a massive structure more than 12 stories high that includes a huge bronze statue of Lady Liberty with wings and carrying a torch with an eternal flame. The structure would include an observation deck with views to the east and west, an 'occupied roof' and two mezzanines.Inside the arch are rooms for program space, offices, a staff lounge, circular staircases, multiple elevators and a 'fire command center.' The project proposes significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic on nearby roads. Administration officials have said the arch also will have a national security function.Chutkan asked what the urgency was and how the government would be harmed 'apart from the executive's desire to bedazzle the city' if she issues a preliminary injunction while the lawsuit plays out. Administration lawyer Robert Stander said the arch was 'absolutely a high priority project' and were Chutkan to step in, that would impede the work of the government.Golf course and Kennedy Center projects also have wound up in courtThe lawsuits are among several that have been filed against the government as Trump seeks to remake the nation's capital at breakneck speed, prompting judges and plaintiffs to balk.U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said Friday she would open a 'formal inquiry' to investigate if federal attorneys violated ethical boundaries, including making misrepresentations to the court, during a legal dispute about the East Potomac Golf Link project. Trump wants the public course overhauled so it could host professional tournaments.There is a hearing Tuesday before U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper on a motion from Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board, seeking the release of communications between the center's management and administration officials. The government has refused so far, citing executive privilege. Trump is the board chair.Beatty alleged in a separate filing Friday that the government withheld information from trustees, including an analysis from the construction manager, that would have shown that a closure was not necessary. She is challenging a government request that Cooper dissolve an injunction he put in place to stop plans to shutter the performing arts venue for two years for renovation. That injunction also called for the removal of Trump's name, which had been placed on the center in December.

news.title: Japan, U.S., Australia, India take aim at China's economic policies
news.text:
During a meeting of the so-called Quad grouping in Atlanta, Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi and his counterparts from the three countries also committed to providing over $85 million in technical and financial assistance to improve access to trusted artificial intelligence across the Indo-Pacific region.

Motegi, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar assessed progress made on ongoing Quad initiatives on the sidelines of a Group of 20 foreign ministers' meeting.

In a joint document issued after their discussions, Motegi, Rubio, Wong and Jaishankar said they had voiced "grave concerns regarding economic coercion, including through arbitrary export restrictions, as well as non-market policies and practices that result in overcapacity to disrupt global supply chains in critical industries."

The top diplomats met for a third time this year ahead of a potential Quad summit next month in the Philippines.

The leaders of Japan, the United States, Australia and India are set to visit Manila in mid-November for meetings involving the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and its partners.

The last Quad summit was held in September 2024, when U.S. President Donald Trump's predecessor Joe Biden was in office. The four-way group sought to organize a leaders' meeting in India last year, but the plan did not materialize due to strains in New Delhi's relations with Washington.

The Quad is often seen as a counterweight to China's growing influence in the Indo-Pacific.

While the Quad's areas of cooperation have been expanding in recent years, from maritime security and critical minerals to health protection and emerging technologies, China has criticized the grouping's initiatives as aimed at containing the country's rise in the region.

On Saturday, among other issues, the top diplomats coordinated views on the situation in the Indo-Pacific, including developments in the South and East China seas, as well as the situation in the Middle East, according to Japan's Foreign Ministry.

During the meeting, Motegi voiced "strong opposition to any attempt to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force or intimidation," the ministry said, adding that the four reaffirmed the importance of advancing their partnership to realize a free and open Indo-Pacific.

Rubio insisted that the Quad is not intended to be against any country.

"To the extent we express concern about things in the Quad, it's concern about behaviors. It's concern about activities. Now, those activities or behaviors are coming repetitively from one country," Rubio told a press conference. "That's going to be obvious to everybody. But it is not an anti-China or anti-anybody coalition."

According to the joint document, to advance "commercial diplomacy," the top diplomats agreed to launch a joint business forum, convening industry leaders, government officials and policy experts from the four countries, to strengthen ties between their public and private sectors.

As part of the initiative, Quad export credit agencies are scheduled to gather in Tokyo on Nov. 18 to identify opportunities for deepening economic cooperation.
