news.title: From fridges to nuclear power plants, hackers are gaining control
news.text:
In the year 2000, on the sleepy banks of the Maroochy River on Queensland's Sunshine Coast, a new water treatment facility was experiencing technical difficulties.

Radio communications to wastewater pumps were not working, and the alarms designed to alert staff were not sounding.

Over a three-month period, more than 800,000 litres of untreated sewage was released into local waterways.

At first, council staff attributed the pump malfunctions to growing pains at the new plant.

But the real culprit? A hacker.

In the same year Australia cemented itself on the global stage hosting the first Olympics of the new millennia, it also secured its spot in the world of cybersecurity as the home of the first attributable case of operational technology hacking, becoming a case study used by engineers, academics and governments to this day.

Cyber-retribution a new war front

Operational technology (OT) is the hardware and software that monitors and controls physical machines.

OT is everywhere and is used to operate critical infrastructure such as power plants, conveyor belts, traffic lights, air traffic control systems and water treatment plants.

The Maroochy incident was 26 years ago, but OT hacking is now on the rise and will likely be supercharged by AI.

Earlier this month, hackers remotely raised fridge and freezer temperatures across hundreds of French supermarkets.

In July, 30 water systems across the United States were attacked, consistent with methods used by an Iranian-backed hacking group the CyberAv3ngers.

In June, a cyber security incident brought Australia's second-largest raw sugar producer to a halt, shutting down milling and cane haulage. A Russian-speaking group called The Gentleman claimed responsibility.

In March, the Handala Hack group, also said to be operating under the Iranian government, claimed responsibility for cyber attacks against medical equipment supplier Stryker. 

Since US President Donald Trump launched the war in Iran, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has issued warnings regarding "ongoing Iranian-affiliated cyber targeting".

In other words: cyber-retribution.

Hacking has become targeted, a new war front for enemies across the globe to attack each other.

The Stryker hack was in retribution for the bombing of an elementary school in southern Iran.

Although the hackers targeted a US company, the attack put Australian hospitals on alert because it remotely wiped associated devices around the world.

Such attacks have obvious financial impacts, but as the technology powering them becomes more sophisticated, the scope and severity of the risks increase.

And as the world destabilises, incentives for hackers to cause harm, including the risk to human life, also increases.

Hacking goes nuclear

In 2025, hackers sponsored by China breached more than 400 agencies across the globe via Microsoft's SharePoint.

One of the agencies was the US National Nuclear Security Administration, the organisation responsible for managing the United States's nuclear stockpile, as well as the nuclear power plants on warships and submarines.

Although an IT hack, not an OT attack, Raji Rajagopalan, a senior fellow at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, explained that such breaches could be used to conduct an OT hack later.

"They get into a system, lie dormant for a very long time and when there is an opportunity, get into sensitive areas," Dr Rajagopalan said.

One protection that nuclear facilities use to prevent such a disaster is an air gap, meaning that administrative systems are largely disconnected from operating systems.

However, Dr Rajagopalan said the assumption that these separations were watertight was not entirely true.

"There are digital upgrades, remote monitoring. All of these always compromise that air gap," she said.

A hacker remotely triggering a nuclear meltdown may sound like the work of Hollywood, but one known incident proved it is closer to reality than fiction.

Stuxnet is a highly sophisticated computer worm.

It was designed as part of Operation Olympic Games, a secret US-Israeli joint cyber-sabotage campaign — although the US government has never publicly taken responsibility.

Stuxnet was unleashed on the Natanz Iranian nuclear facility, where it lay undetected between 2009-2010.

The worm targeted the centrifuges used to enrich uranium, causing them to spin out of control until they broke. It was also sophisticated enough to hide what it was doing.

Stuxnet destroyed at least 1,000 centrifuges at Natanz and set Iran's nuclear program back by about a year.

Such attacks make global headlines when they are discovered, causing policymakers to make sweeping statements at press conferences.

But, Dr Rajagopalan said, political momentum was often lost after the fact.

"You don't want to scare people away, but at the same time, people need to understand that there are consequences to these attacks, that these attacks are real."

Critical infrastructure a sitting duck

Why is OT so vulnerable? How is it that the most critical infrastructure in the world is so at risk of being hacked?

UQ cyber security expert Ryan Ko said the main issue with OT was that much of it had been installed 20 to 30 years ago before existing knowledge of the latest cyber threats.

The old legacy systems were increasingly connected to the internet, he said, and every piece of critical infrastructure connected with OT was at risk.

And with the rise of AI, the scope of cyber-attacks had "changed drastically".

"It is now easier for an adversary to automatically detect a previously unknown vulnerability," Professor Ko said.

OpenAI's rogue agent Medicare data portal hack raised significant alarms for the Australian government.

Although not an OT attack, the incident highlighted how AI can efficiently find weaknesses that in other circumstances could be leveraged by bad faith actors.

Domestically, the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) provides frameworks for governments and businesses to boost their cyber-defences against what it has described as "increasingly complex and persistent threats".

"Critical infrastructure and operational technology are attractive targets for state-sponsored cyber actors, cyber criminals and hacktivists," an ASD spokesperson said.

Can we stop OT spiralling out of control?

Dr Rajagopalan said as OT hacking incidents increased, the possibility of inadvertent incidents spiralling out of control also increased.

It is a scenario where neither side may want to engage in "big open-ended conflict, but things going out of control".

In a fracturing world, not only does the current geopolitical climate increase the incentive for enemies to attack one other, but it also limits the ability for allies to work with each other.

One solution for Australia, Dr Rajagopalan said, could be partnering with multilateral organisations such as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations over major powers.

"Bring together smaller groupings of countries who have similar or like-minded interests and who have a certain amount of appeal to international law," she said.
news.summary: Hackers are breaking into more than computers. They are taking control of the physical machines that have underpinned our lives for decades.

Atlanta: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Saturday said there was growing interest by the international community in facilitating a limited ceasefire in the Black Sea to ensure unfettered energy and grain shipments by Russia and Ukraine.Rubio told a news conference that the US is reviewing proposals by Turkey and India to get grain shipments moving, even as the US continues to press for a broader, negotiated settlement of the war, which is now in its fifth year.Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine took center stage at a two-day meeting of foreign ministers from the Group of 20, in part due to the participation of Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov over the objections of European and Canadian leaders, who argued that including him normalized Russia's aggression.The meeting ended without a joint statement or agreement on the myriad issues facing the world's largest economies.Rubio defended the invitation of Lavrov, saying it would be impossible to end the war diplomatically without talking with Russia, but admitting that such a deal was not on the immediate horizon. He said the US spoke frequently with Ukrainian leaders, although Ukraine's foreign minister was not invited.Live EventsHe said there was growing interest - if not momentum - in partial deals such as halting attacks on ships carrying grain and, in some cases, energy, in the Black Sea."This is threatening the world for food security and some energy security as well," Rubio told reporters after a two-day meeting of foreign ministers from the world's 20 largest economies, which revealed big rifts over the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East."We'd like to achieve it. It doesn't solve the war, but at least it solves a unique aspect of it," Rubio said, adding that a negotiated settlement remained a top priority for US officials, despite the failure to get there yet."There's a very nasty war going on, a very destructive war," Rubio said, adding that the war was already threatening to escalate to other countries given irregular efforts at sabotage and drone strikes that wandered into NATO airspace.Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand told Reuters in an interview that she would not have chosen to invite Lavrov, but she used the occasion to confront him directly about Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022."I stared him in the eye and called out Russia's further illegal invasion of Ukraine, the stealing of Ukrainian children, the targeting of Ukrainian ships in the Black Sea, all of which are reprehensible, all of which are contrary to international law and international humanitarian law," Anand said, citing her remarks during a closed-door plenary session on Friday.Anand said she had spoken with Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, as well as her counterpart from India, about enacting a limited ceasefire in the Black Sea and putting a moratorium on attacks on Ukraine's electrical infrastructure.Anand said a number of interlocutors were pushing for some kind of ceasefire, with a huge focus on shoring up food supply chains and brokering an end to attacks on Ukraine's electrical grid and energy infrastructure before the coming winter."We have to address these issues now as Ukraine approaches the winter," she said, noting that Canada had been engaged in significant and specific talks about a Black Sea ceasefire since the United Nations General Assembly in September.India and Egypt were two countries that were heavily affected, and wanted to ensure that their own ships - and sailors - remained safe. Ukraine was fully engaged on the issue, but Russia had not shown it was willing to move ahead, she said.Lavrov on Friday told reporters that Moscow's position on the Ukraine conflict was unchanged, and Russia could not accept Ukraine as a "military threat to the lawful security interests of the Russian Federation," according to Russian news agencies.Rubio urged G20 participants on Friday to cooperate where possible given the complex web of economic and geopolitical challenges facing nearly every country."Because we all face these challenges, we must all work together to address them," he said. "The future of our nations depends on our willingness to understand that while our interests may not always align, we should always seek to work together to advance them when and where they do align."Rubio told reporters that he spoke briefly with Lavrov on the sidelines of the meeting about the opportunity for US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to meet at the APEC meeting next month and the G20 leaders summit to be held at Trump's Doral golf resort in Miami in December.Rubio said there was no firm commitment for Putin to attend the G20 summit. news.title: Russia responds to US warning of Moscow attack plan
news.text:
Russia's FSB security service says it has carried out "appropriate" measures after the US embassy in Moscow warned of a planned "terrorist" attack in the capital this weekend.

The US embassy said earlier it was "aware of a credible threat of a mass-casualty event" on Saturday, local time, at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve in Moscow.

The US government had coordinated "with appropriate Russian authorities on a response", it said.

It advised people: "Avoid the area, stay alert, and avoid crowds."

The US embassy did not give details on who was plotting the attack.

The Tsaritsyno museum is an imperial palace and park complex that is a popular place to visit in southern Moscow, especially on weekends.

Russian Telegram channel Baza, which reportedly has links to law enforcement, said the park was now closed and "open only for exits".

Russia's FSB security service said earlier it had received information from the US "regarding the preparation of a terrorist attack".

"Appropriate work is underway," it was quoted as saying by Russian news agencies.

In March 2024, the US Embassy warned that extremists had imminent plans for an attack in Moscow. 

Days later, gunmen attacked the Crocus City Hall concert venue outside Moscow, killing more than 140 people.

The latest sharing of information underlines the increasingly close relationship between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Despite Moscow's continuing war against Ukraine, Mr Trump has appeared more accommodating towards the Kremlin than America's traditional European allies.

Last month, Mr Trump struck a controversial deal to purchase Russian diesel, reversing years of Western efforts to isolate Moscow economically. 

The agreement could provide Mr Putin with billions of dollars to sustain his war.

Meanwhile, European media reports that Mr Putin will accept Mr Trump's invitation and attend December's G20 summit in the US.

Mr Putin has not attended a G20 summit since 2019, with Russia ejected from the more exclusive G8 after its annexation of Crimea in 2014.

The traditional "family photo" at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta this weekend — a picture of all the gathered ministers, taken at each edition of the event — was cancelled after multiple US allies, including Australia, refused to be photographed alongside Mr Putin's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.
news.summary: Russia's FSB security service says it has carried out "appropriate" measures after the US embassy in Moscow warned of a planned "terrorist" attack in the capital this weekend.

news.title: Judge dismisses Trump lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein cartoon
news.text:
A federal judge has thrown out US President Donald Trump's $US10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

US District Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed the lawsuit filed in Miami, saying the president was "grasping at straws".

Judge Gayles ruled the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law and the suit had attempted to "manufacture" flaws in the newspaper's reporting. 

The lawsuit against the Journal was over a story it published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the paper said bore Mr Trump's name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein's 50th birthday.

The letter was reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell as part of a birthday album for Epstein years before he was first arrested in 2006 and subsequently had a falling-out with Mr Trump.

Mr Trump denied writing it and called the story "false, malicious, and defamatory".

The case was thrown out "with prejudice", which means it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent. 

Here's what to know. 

Trump calls out 'malicious' reporting

The letter bearing Mr Trump's name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, "Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret", according to the newspaper.

In his lawsuit, Mr Trump called the alleged birthday greeting "fake" and sought $US10 billion ($14 billion) for what he called damage to his reputation.

News Corp's Dow Jones, the Journal's parent, defended the accuracy of its July 17, 2025, article.

The lawsuit was one of several Mr Trump has filed in his second term against major media outlets over reporting he has characterised as unfair or false.

In asking Judge Gayles to dismiss the case in September, lawyers for the Journal and its billionaire owner Rupert Murdoch wrote that the lawsuit threatened to chill the speech of those who publish content that Mr Trump does not like.

Wasn't the case already dismissed?

Donald Trump's case, originally filed July 18, 2025 against The Wall Street Journal, was thrown out by the same judge, Darrin Gayles, in April of this year.

He said the article did not meet the "actual malice" standard that public figures must clear in defamation.

They must prove not only that a public statement about them was false but also that the media outlet or person who made the statement knew or should have known that it was false.

"This complaint comes nowhere close to this standard," Judge Gayles wrote. 

"Quite the opposite."

Mr Trump was then allowed to refile the lawsuit which he did later that month. 

According to the amended lawsuit, Mr Trump called Mr Murdoch on July 15, 2025 after Journal reporters contacted the White House about the story.

"In response, Murdoch stated, 'I will handle it,' which President Trump reasonably interpreted as meaning that Murdoch believed President Trump, and that the article would not be published," the lawsuit says.

Representatives of Dow Jones did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the filing or on the allegation regarding Mr Murdoch.

Dow Jones, which News Corp owns, previously said it had full confidence in the Journal's reporting and will defend itself in court.

Mr Murdoch is chairman emeritus of News Corp.

How has the case been permanently thrown out?

In the US, a case being thrown out "with prejudice" means it is permanently over and there is no reason to bring it back to court. 

In Saturday's ruling, the judge cited the Supreme Court's landmark 1964 ruling in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. 

That decision made it harder for public figures to win libel lawsuits because it requires proof that a media outlet knowingly published something false or showed a reckless disregard for the truth.

“The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice," Judge Gayles wrote.

"Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false."

The judge also noted that the Journal's story did not ignore or minimise Mr Trump's denial.

"Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it."

Judge Gayles also said several other allegations in the lawsuit did not have merit.
news.summary: The judge presiding over Donald Trump's lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch throws it out, claiming the US president attempted to "manufacture" flaws in the news outlet's investigative reporting.
news.author: Georgie Hewson

news.title: Why Trump’s White House Is About to Get Very Ugly: Author
news.text:
The battle for influence around President Donald Trump will turn into a bloodbath as his second term winds down and Democrats threaten to weaken his power after the midterms, his longtime biographer predicted. 

Author Michael Wolff speculated that more and more people would jockey for influence in the president’s inner circle—even after former Justice Department official Alina Habba was busted locking down a $50 million deal with the family of a scandal-ridden Venezuelan billionaire who later secured a pardon from Trump.

A bombshell report by The New York Times earlier revealed that the family of Julio Herrera Velutini, a billionaire banker from Venezuela, hired then-DOJ adviser Habba as general counsel for a shadowy company called Concord Partners. Weeks later, Trump granted Herrera Velutini a full and unconditional pardon over a misdemeanor campaign finance violation.

Wolff said the controversy was a reflection of the broader “Donald Trump ecosystem.”

“It’s all about influence,” he told Inside Trump’s Head co-host Joanna Coles. “Strong men in a kind of authoritarian, despotic roles, that’s what they do, is that they sell their influence. That’s how they maintain their power, is by putting it up for grabs for other people to make money off of. So everybody then makes money off of this central power in the middle. And that’s also what happens with Donald Trump.”

“But that’s what so many other people around Donald Trump are also doing,” he continued. “And this is going to get more intense as the end comes for the Trump administration—and the feeling may be that it is ending much sooner with Tuesday’s election—is that everybody is going to be so much more focused on getting what they can while the getting is good, which is going to increase the pressure, increase the the resentments, increase the competition around Trump, and it’s going to be bloody.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this story. Previously, White House spokesman Davis Ingle told the Daily Beast: “Michael Wolff is a professional scumbag and serial liar whose brain has been completely warped by his severe and incurable disease known as Trump Derangement Syndrome.”

Habba, the DOJ, and the White House have all vigorously contested The Times’ reporting.

“Any insinuation that my employment — all of which has been vetted and disclosed to the D.O.J. — had anything to do with securing a pardon is false and defamatory,” Habba wrote in one of two statements posted on social media.

Habba, a former Trump lawyer, stepped down as U.S. Attorney for the District of New Jersey last year after a court ruled that she had been unlawfully serving for too long without Senate confirmation.

The White House similarly said Habba had nothing to do with the pardon, adding to the Times that the administration follows a pardon review process that includes the White House Counsel’s Office and the DOJ.

The Daily Beast did not receive a response from Concord Partners and Herrera Velutini.

The Times’ exposé sent Trump into a fit of rage, according to subsequent reporting from the outlet. Trump told aides and allies that Habba should donate a portion of the $50 million to his future presidential library or another Trump-linked entity, insiders said.

Habba, meanwhile, has remained defiant.

“I was never paid to secure a pardon. I never met with anyone at the White House or DOJ about a pardon. I’ve never done any work in any capacity whatsoever for a pardon for anyone, period,” she wrote on X.

Author Michael Wolff speculated that more and more people would jockey for influence in the president’s inner circle—even after former Justice Department official Alina Habba was busted locking down a $50 million deal with the family of a scandal-ridden Venezuelan billionaire who later secured a pardon from Trump.

news.title: Trump agrees to visa for mother of Ghanaian teen killed in New York, Mamdani says
news.text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has claimed in a social media post that President Donald Trump has agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a 15-year-old immigrant from Ghana who was shot dead earlier this week.
The White House did not immediately respond to an e-mail from The Associated Press confirming the administration would be issuing the visa.
The teen, Javits Frimpong, was on his way to school in a Bronx neighbourhood shortly before 9.30 am on Thursday when he was shot in the abdomen, New York City police said. He was pronounced dead at a hospital later that day. No arrests have yet been made, and the killing remains under investigation.
“The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away,” Mamdani wrote Saturday on X. “Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump, and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately.”
“All of New York City is mourning this tragedy,” he said.
Frimpong arrived in the Bronx from Ghana a year ago to be with his father and begin a new life in the United States, according to US Rep. Ritchie Torres, a Democrat from the Bronx.
Frimpong was on his way to school when he was shot, Torres wrote on X.
“Our entire borough is mourning a young man who should have had his whole future ahead of him,” Torres said. “Every child in the Bronx deserves to walk to school without fearing for their life, and no parent should ever have to endure what Javits’s father, Thomas, is enduring now.”
Foreign Minister Sam Okudzeto Ablakwa said in a post on X that Ghanaian officials in New York are coordinating with local authorities and that the foreign ministry “will work tirelessly with US authorities to ensure justice is secured.”
Trump has clamped down on immigration during his second term, including suspending the processing of visas from 75 countries.
(This is an agency story. Except for the headline, the story has not been edited by Firstpost staff.)

news.title: Policy Drift
news.text:
By Malay Mishra

Ever since India announced the standardisation of 28 places in Ladakh in accordance with the Survey of India’s demarcation, China’s behaviour towards India has changed markedly. The Centre’s revocation of Article 370 and declaration of Ladakh as a Union Territory on August 5, 2019, had drawn sharp criticism from Beijing. A Chinese spokesperson has since reportedly claimed all of eastern Ladakh, unsettling Delhi amid a thaw in bilateral ties. India seeks a larger role globally, even as dependence on Chinese intermediates contributes to a trade deficit of $112 billion.

During Xi’s recent visit to Delhi for the BRICS Summit (September 12-13), and earlier at the BRICS summit in Kazan in 2024 and the SCO summit in Tianjin in 2025, he and Modi appeared to develop a rapport that could have advanced understanding on the boundary dispute. China’s renewed reference to the November 1959 claim line, set out in Zhou Enlai’s letter to Nehru and rejected before the 1962 war, is a retrograde step. Delhi appears caught between two powers.

After visiting India, Xi received a lavish welcome from US President Donald Trump in Washington. Trump’s G2 idea of a US-China entente seemingly diminished India’s strategic importance to Washington. Beijing also secured Trump’s acquiescence to freezing a $14-billion arms package for Taiwan. The PLA turns 100 in 2027. Since occupying the Shaksgam Valley in 1963, Beijing has consolidated its position near Siachen and linked it to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), spending $1 billion. CPEC passes through Gilgit-Baltistan, which India claims as part of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. In October, the Pakistani and Chinese armies reportedly began the Karakoram exercises after signing a Joint Border Military Commission agreement. This has reinforced the perception that India may face a single China-Pakistan front rather than two separate fronts, changing the nature of a possible multi-pronged conflict.

On the eastern frontier, Arunachal Pradesh has faced alleged PLA incursions. ITBP Director General Shatrujit Kapur recently said face-offs had continued since July. His remarks at an ITBP function in Rajasthan were ostensibly aimed at securing advanced drones for the force’s new Shaurya regiment. A report in The Hindu said Chinese forces had moved 6-7 km into Indian territory and occupied grazing areas used by local tribes. The MEA acknowledged face-offs in Upper Subansiri, saying they were being addressed diplomatically and militarily.

China is also reportedly building an 11,200-MW mega dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo, the upper Brahmaputra, in the Siang region, near its entry into India where it joins the Dibang and Lohit. India is pursuing the 1,605-MW Subansiri Upper Hydroelectric Project, or Menga Dam. Observers warn that the lack of a clear response could invite a Galwan-like eastern crisis.

In Ladakh, meanwhile, the Leh Apex Body and Kargil Democratic Alliance, along with civil society groups, are demanding greater autonomy, a legislature and constitutional safeguards under Article 371, which they say were promised by the Centre during talks on May 22.

Against this backdrop, US Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio’s October 20-22 business-focused visit was seen as another snub to Delhi. He bypassed the capital for Mumbai, where External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar joined him for talks on energy, trade, investment and defence, as well as events marking America’s 250th anniversary. The UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister joined them for discussions on I2U2 and the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), initiatives involving India, the UAE, Israel and the US.

Rubio was also seeking fuel supplies amid concerns over Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi threats to Bab el-Mandeb shipping. In Jamnagar, Rubio met Mukesh Ambani and his family at the industrialist’s refinery. Details were not disclosed. He may have urged the group to expedite its proposed $300-billion Texas refinery.

Washington also wants to fast-track a US-India trade agreement. US demands for market access could provoke India’s farm and manufacturing sectors. India’s services sector faces sharply higher H-1B visa fees; JD Vance’s description of Indian IT workers as “indentured servants” drew no official response.

Trump’s temporary waiver of sanctions provisions relating to Russian and Iranian oil purchases, alongside his reported plans to buy 300 million tonnes of diesel from Russia, must also be viewed in this wider context.

India’s strategic autonomy is under strain as Washington appears to accommodate Pakistan. Islamabad is meanwhile building Islamic partnerships: the Mecca Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey has reportedly expanded into the Badr Agreement, involving Indonesia and Qatar, with Bangladesh showing interest. India’s ambition, often voiced by foreign-policy experts, to become the pole star of the Global South through multipolarity and multi-alignment may therefore have to wait.

Domestic challenges compound the external ones: inflation, unemployment, declining savings and a farm crisis, alongside paper-leak scandals, alleged Ayodhya temple embezzlement and concerns over voters’ rights and ECI manipulation. A government increasingly on the defensive struggles to anchor India’s external relations. The nation is indeed facing its hardest-ever test conflating both external and domestic crises into a serious challenge for India’s democracy.

The writer is a former Ambassador.

news.title: California governor asks US judges to resist Trump attempts to seize ballots
news.text: p>San Francisco: California Governor Gavin Newsom on Saturday warned federal courts to be ready for potential attempts by President Donald Trump's administration to seize ballots during the upcoming midterm elections.Newsom, a Democrat, sent the warning letter to federal judges as the state's legal fight with the administration, which demanded records from California as part of a criminal investigation into noncitizen voting. On Friday, a US appeals court rejected the administration's bid, potentially setting up a showdown at the US Supreme Court.Separately, a federal judge ordered the Justice Department to stop threatening to prosecute state and local election officials in California who refuse to comply with the administration's election-related demands."Given the United States Department of Justice’s persistence in advancing this baseless theory of criminal liability, I have grave concerns federal agents will seek search warrants to seize ballots and ballot materials before the election results are certified," Newsom wrote..Like Hema Malini in Mathura, a dummy candidate has emerged in Alaska - but it’s not a joke for Donald Trump.The only reason to use search warrants would be to interfere in the state's "lawful counting of ballots and certifying the results of the election," Newsom wrote to the federal judges.The US Constitution assigns the administration of elections to the states, but the Trump administration has alleged that more than 20,000 noncitizens are registered to vote in California, though the state and many experts have questioned the validity of the list. The Justice Department has not said how many of the people on its list have actually submitted ballots.California has said the Justice Department's assertions relied ⁠on "suspect data" ​and that complying with its demands would risk disenfranchising eligible voters.</p

news.title: Ex-Mossad agent assisted Flavio Bolsonaro's escape from Brazil after election defeat: Report
news.text:
A former Mossad agent, who became a naturalised citizen of the United States, reportedly helped Brazil's Senator Flavio Bolsonaro flee the country after his election defeat. The revalation was made by a CNN Brazil report that cited findings from a security agency investigation in Brazil. The son of the country's former president, Jair Bolsonaro, arrived in Miami, violating a judicial order that barred him from leaving the country.
As per the report, the operation was planned prior to the second round of the presidential election and involved assistance from figures in Argentina and the United States. The investigators noted that the former Israeli intelligence officer, whose identity has not been disclosed, arrived in Brazil on October 19, six days before the second round of the presidential election.
He then accompanied Bolsonaro from the capital, Brasília, to the border with Argentina and remained in the vehicle with him during the border crossing. According to CNN Brazil, the country's investigators identified two commercial vans that crossed the Tancredo Neves Bridge connecting Foz do Iguaçu in Brazil to Puerto Iguazú in Argentina via security camera footage on Tuesday.
As per the report, Bolsonaro and the former Mossad agent travelled in one vehicle, while his wife and two daughters travelled in the second. One driver was identified as a former municipal council member from Foz do Iguaçu, and the second driver was his son.
The Journey from Argentina to the US
After crossing the border, the team then boarded a Gulfstream G400 executive jet operated by the Argentine airline Baires Fly. The aircraft then took off for the United States, refuelled in Guayaquil, Ecuador, and landed Wednesday morning at Opa-locka Executive Airport near Miami.
In a separate report by The New York Times, Jason Miller, a political strategist close to US President Donald Trump, helped arrange the aircraft. Apart from this, Argentine newspaper Clarín reported that Santiago Caputo, a top advisor to Argentine President Javier Milei, arrived in the border area to oversee the operation and prevent documentation of the crossing.
It is pertinent to note that Bolsonaro lost to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of elections on October 25. After the elections, Brazil's Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered the confiscation of Bolsonaro's passports and barred him from leaving the country.
The senator has been under investigation for suspected money laundering, including a case involving gambling platforms and another regarding the funding of a film about his father. The allegations have not been proven in court. The Federal Police stated that no official record was found of the senator's departure through Brazilian border control checkpoints.

news.title: US judge dismisses Trump lawsuit against Wall Steet Journal over Epstein letter
news.text:
APA US judge dismissed Donald Trump's defamation lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch

Washington: A US judge on Saturday dismissed President Donald Trump's defamation lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and media magnate Rupert Murdoch over a report that Trump sent a bawdy birthday letter to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.Trump had sued for $10 billion after the newspaper's story was published in July 2025 detailing the president's alleged 2003 letter to Epstein, which apparently featured a drawing of a naked woman.Murdoch is the founder of News Corp. which owns the Wall Street Journal.The report piled scrutiny on Trump from both Democrats and his own Republican party, who rejected the president's attempts to downplay the saga as a hoax and called for a full release of legal files on Epstein.In Saturday's ruling, Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed Trump's lawsuit with prejudice, meaning Trump cannot file an amended version of the suit, as he did when Gayles turned down an initial version of it back in April.Live EventsThe judge wrote that in bringing his defamation claim, Trump had both times failed to establish that the defendants "acted with actual malice."The House Oversight Committee last year published a copy of Trump's alleged birthday note to Epstein, which consists of a short dialogue between "Donald" and "Jeffrey.""We have certain things in common," says Donald, to which Jeffrey responds: "Yes, we do, come to think of it.""Enigmas never age, have you noticed that?" asks Donald."As a matter of fact, it was clear to me the last time I saw you," says Jeffrey."A pal is a wonderful thing. Happy Birthday -- and may every day be another wonderful secret," the note ends, followed by Trump's signature, which takes the place of pubic hair on the nude outline.Epstein files Trump's supporters have been obsessed with the Epstein case for years and held as an article of faith that "deep state" elites were protecting a sex ring of Epstein associates, particularly in the Democratic Party and Hollywood.The president fought for months to prevent the Department of Justice from releasing the so-called "Epstein Files" but eventually signed a law passed by Congress requiring their publication.Trump's name appears repeatedly in the documents but he denies any wrongdoing and has not been charged with any criminal offenses connected to the affair.High-profile figures including Britain's former prince Andrew have been publicly disgraced for their associations with Epstein.Ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections which will decide control of Congress, Democrats have reportedly spent more than $35 million on Epstein-related advertisements.With a Republican majority in the House and Senate, Trump has so far enjoyed relatively little political opposition since taking office in January 2025, giving the courts a key role in limiting him.In a separate case Saturday, a new suit was filed to prevent Trump's attempt to erect a huge triumphal arch in front of the iconic military cemetery outside Washington.That is one of a number of projects launched by Trump in a bid to put his personal stamp on the capital, including a ballroom at the White House and a laborious renovation of the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: The Dems catering to the extremists ahead of Election Day is another victory for the far-left
news.text:
For decades, an evergreen media storyline has been that the next election will resolve the civil war between the center and far-left factions of the Democratic Party. 

The thumb-sucking chatter continues even as the victor of the current round is obvious. 

Before all midterm votes are cast and counted, we have a clear winner — it’s the far left, because once again the center didn’t hold. 

As is their habit, relatively moderate Dems folded without much of a fight, and so the radicals did not need to seize every slot to win the internal struggle. 

All they had to do was have a relative few fresh-faced hard-liners stake out positions beyond the pale, make a lot of noise and enjoy the ride as the media dubbed them the table setters of the future. 

Some of the old guard leadership briefly resisted, but to little avail. 

Their capitulation illustrates why moderate Dems are getting dumped into the dustbins of history as the radicals gobble up more ground each election cycle. 

They all hate Israel, want exorbitant taxes, favor coddling criminals, opening the borders and swelling the size and reach of government while imposing restrictions on individual liberty. 

‘Party consensus’ 

As New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani summed up the Socialist vision in his January inaugural address, “We will replace the frigidity of rugged individualism with the warmth of collectivism.” 

Shortly after that, 20 homeless New Yorkers froze to death on Gotham’s streets during a harsh winter. 

A related lesson comes from former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who is voluntarily leaving Congress after 20 terms and 40 years. 

Widely admired for her ruthless ability to herd cats on key legislation, she heads back to California with hopes Dems win both chambers this week. 

But on a podcast, she added a wrinkle. 

As The New York Times reported her comments, she insisted that those on the far left who are attacking Israel “don’t represent the consensus of the party” as it seeks congressional control. 

She cited Mamdani and Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and said those who do not support Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state are not just “concerning — it’s wrong.” 

I certainly agree with her on that, but she then veered deep into the partisan mindset by saying the virulent positions on Israel do not stop her from wanting the radicals to win. 

“This new person in Michigan, we’ll see if he gets elected to the Congress,” she said about El-Sayed. 

“But the mayor, bless his heart, I hope he succeeds as mayor. But I don’t agree with some of the things he has said.” 

She justified her support by hiding behind the fig leaf claim that neither man represents the majority of the party. 

In effect, she’s willing to swallow their antisemitism because their victories would give Dems more power. 

“We have to win big, so that doesn’t really matter,” she added about their positions on Israel. 

Got it. Antisemitism and a history of supporting Islamist terrorists are no big deal when you have an election to win and a government to control. 

Pelosi first crossed that bridge during her last years as speaker when radical Reps. Ilhan Omar, Rashida Talib, Jamaal Bowman and Cori Bush openly espoused their hate for Israel, police and anyone who dared to vote for Donald Trump. 

‘Big tentism’ 

Pelosi didn’t ex-communicate them or even publicly draw a line. Instead, she welcomed them and eagerly sought their support on other issues. 

Chuck Schumer, the Dem Senate leader, is similarly malleable. 

El-Sayed criticized him relentlessly and, as The Post reports, spoke and campaigned at Michigan mosques where speakers called for the end of the Zionist state and the death of Jews. 

Although Schumer had endorsed El-Sayed’s primary opponent, he quickly joined the parade when El-Sayed captured the nomination. 

Despite the fact that Schumer, the highest elected Jewish official in American history, long portrayed himself as the guardian of Israel, he glibly justified his support for El-Sayed. 

Asked about his conversion, he said Dems must be “a big tent party,” and advocated “big tentism” because “it’s how you build a majority.” 

That attitude apparently extends to Hasan Piker, El-Sayed’s America-hating buddy and Twitch streamer. 

He doesn’t even like his friend’s campaign workers trying to drum up support in heavily Jewish Michigan neighborhoods. 

“This has got to be the wildest door-knocking operation of all time,” Piker said. 

“Trying to get perhaps the most Zionist district in the country, well, not the most, but one of the more Zionist wealthy districts in the country to vote for a Muslim anti-Zionist. Brave soldiers, all of them.” 

He also called it the “equivalent of going to that Klan KKK neighborhood for a black candidate who’s running to abolish anti-miscegenation laws.” 

How charming. 

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul illustrates another example of the corrupting influence of ambition.

Years ago, Hochul was a conservative-leaning upstate official as her party swung left. 

Those credentials led Gov. Andrew Cuomo to make her his running mate in 2014 and 2018, when he wanted a boost from the right. 

She succeeded him when he was forced to resign in 2021, and won her own term in 2022. 

Her victory was a nail-biter, and she seemingly concluded there was no future in moderation as most of the party followed the left-ward anti-Trump lurch. 

Opportunistic 

Capturing the spirit of Tammany Hall boss George Washington Plunkitt, who said a century ago that “I seen my opportunities and I took ’em,” Hochul saw which way the wind was blowing and joined the parade. 

Her ambition spiked at an opportunistic time. 

Last year, Mamdani’s social media skills propelled him to victory as the Pied Piper of a new generation of leftist voters. 

Many Dem officials shunned him, but Hochul endorsed him. 

When he took office, she took on the role of his Big Sister and powerful collaborator. 

She funded his crackpot spending and taxing ideas, and he is responding by becoming her sidekick in the closing days of her campaign.

news.title: Erdogan slams Black Sea shipping attacks
news.text:
ISTANBUL / WASHINGTON: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said on Saturday that attacks targeting civilian vessels in the Black Sea were unacceptable, urging Russia and Ukraine to “act responsibly”.

Despite its ties with both Russia and Ukraine, Turkiye has been angered by attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea.

“It is clear that attacks against civilian vessels and actions that further escalate tensions in the Black Sea serve no one’s interests,” Erdogan told a news conference with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky in Istanbul.

“We cannot accept these attacks under any circumstances, regardless of who carries them out or what justification is offered. We call on all parties to act responsibly on this matter,” he said.

 Says attacks on civilian vessels ‘unacceptable’; Zelensky discusses security, peace efforts with Turkish president

Ankara has sent a proposal to Russia and Ukraine to end strikes on civilian ships, but says the two countries have failed to act on it.

Zelensky accused Russia of making the situation in the Black Sea difficult, saying a significant part of his talks with Erdogan had focused on security concerns in the region.

Erdogan said discussions aimed at restoring the safety of navigation in the Black Sea would continue.

“I believe that reaching an agreement on this issue would also give fresh impetus to efforts to secure lasting peace in Ukraine,” he added.

Erdogan also welcomed renewed momentum behind efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war through “diplomatic means”, referring in particular to US President Donald Trump’s initiative.

“At this point, we maintain that there can be no losers in a just peace,” he said.

Last week, the Kremlin said the next round of talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US was expected to resume in November in the UAE.

Zelensky said he had discussed the format of the talks with Erdogan, as well as other possibilities, “in particular the possibilities of involving Turkiye, involving Europe, involving all partners”.

Patriot missiles

The Trump administration has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, the US State Department said, but the Ukrainian president warned that deliveries could take years.

The approval, which will be submitted to Congress for review, comes after weeks of complaints by Ukrainian authorities that their supplies of the interceptor missiles were dwindling.

“The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defence capabilities,” the department said in a statement.

The statement did not provide an estimate of when the weapons could be delivered to Ukraine.

However, Zelensky said late on Friday in a post on X that “deliveries may begin only in a few years”.

news.title: Trump Speaks To Netanyahu As US Weighs Fresh Iran Strikes: Report
news.text:
US President Donald Trump spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over the phone on Saturday as Washington weighed the possibility of resuming military action against Iran, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the conversation.
The call followed a White House meeting earlier this week, during which Trump consulted senior military officials on strategic options for restarting major combat operations, the newspaper said.
Amid the possibility of renewed strikes, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said diplomatic engagement with Iran was continuing, but declined to specify a timeline or assess the progress of negotiations. He also said Trump had not yet decided whether to take further military action.
Speaking to reporters after the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Georgia, Rubio said Washington remained open to a diplomatic resolution, provided it addressed US security concerns.
“There are multiple talks; talks have actually never stopped. There's been active conversations going both in some cases directly, but often through intermediaries,” Rubio said.
Rubio Says Trump Yet To Decide On Further Military Action
Responding to questions on how long the US would allow diplomatic efforts to continue before potentially resuming military operations, Rubio said the decision rested with Trump.
“I'm not gonna characterise either the progress on those talks or any timeframe on it other than to tell you that if there is a diplomatic solution, we would be open to it,” he said.
Rubio said any agreement would have to address Washington's concerns over Iran's nuclear ambitions and its support for armed groups across the region.
Asked about the possibility of fresh strikes, the US Secretary of State declined to discuss specific military contingency plans. He said Trump preferred a peaceful resolution but maintained that the US had the capability to achieve its military objectives.
“We can achieve military objectives if we seek to. He hasn't made a decision,” Rubio said.
Rubio also accused Tehran of targeting commercial vessels carrying cargo, oil and natural gas, warning that maritime disruptions could affect economies well beyond the conflict zone.
He said US naval forces were intercepting incoming drones and anti-ship missiles almost every night. However, petroleum transit volumes remained comparable to pre-conflict levels, despite the continuing requirement for security protection.
Warning of wider economic consequences, Rubio said disruptions to maritime trade could threaten global food security by affecting supplies of fuel, agricultural inputs and food commodities.
He also accused Iran of backing Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Houthis and various militias challenging the Iraqi state.
“So anywhere you turn, what you find is some Iranian proxy that's undermining the peace and stability of the Middle East,” he said.
Iran Says US Tone Has Shifted After Vance's Letter
Even as Washington indicated that diplomatic contacts were continuing, Iran's top security official Mohsen Rezaei said the US had changed its approach in a letter sent by Vice President JD Vance, Al Jazeera reported.
“Their tone has shifted completely, which is a good sign that shows that our people have secured their victory,” Rezaei told state broadcaster IRIB.
The letter was delivered to Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, through Qatari mediators on Sunday. According to The New York Times, the proposal envisages direct negotiations under Vance's leadership, with Iran's nuclear programme included in discussions from the outset.
The Wall Street Journal, citing a source, reported that the communication outlined a "framework for negotiations" rather than specific peace terms. It added that the letter had been sent at Trump's direction.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday that Tehran had studied the letter and described Washington's attempt to open dialogue as a "positive step". He also said an aide had travelled to Doha for consultations with mediators.
Citing sources, Al Jazeera reported that a meeting could take place within a week, with Doha and Istanbul being considered as possible venues.
Mojtaba Khamenei Warns Of 'Geographically Unrestricted' Response
Meanwhile, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned that Iran's military would respond to any missteps by the US or Israel with a response that was “geographically unrestricted”.
“If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it is the armed forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine the time and conditions for their end,” Khamenei said.
Trump, speaking at the White House on Friday, had said Tehran was keen to negotiate.
"There are talks, they want to talk, they keep talking," he said, adding, "We have time, frankly."
The US President also claimed that Iran was "in a lot of trouble" and predicted that the conflict would end “very soon”.

news.title: Israeli protesters demand opposition ally with Arab parties to oust Netanyahu
news.text: TEL AVIV, Israel — Hundreds of Israelis took to the streets on Saturday to urge the opposition to ally with Arab parties to oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has gone on the offensive against the minority group's leaders.Arab-majority parties made major gains in Tuesday's election, fuelled by anger over rhetoric targeting the community from Netanyahu's hard-right government, but opposition chief Gadi Eisenkot has not decided whether to seek a coalition with them.Joining a rally in Tel Aviv, Ayelet Raz said that the Arab community, which accounts for around 20 percent of Israel's population, had a right to political participation.'It's the last chance for real change,' the 60-year-old psychologist said, warning that Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, was a 'great manipulator'.'We need to give peace a chance,' she said. 'Otherwise we'll have this bloodshed forever.'Tuesday's election was inconclusive, with neither bloc reaching a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament.Jewish-majority parties opposed to Netanyahu, known by his nickname Bibi, won 48 seats, while two Arab-majority parties, Raam and the Joint List, secured a combined 19 seats.An alliance between the two camps would potentially give the anti-Netanyahu bloc a comfortable majority of 67 seats, but the idea is opposed by some parties in the opposition bloc.'Arabs and Jews will only win together' and 'There is a majority for change' read some of the signs held by around 500 protesters in Tel Aviv.'67 -- United we stand, divided we get Bibi' and 'Why not, really -- unless we are racist?' read some of the placards at the 100-strong rally in Jerusalem.Arab parties have only once formally sat in an Israeli government, when Raam leader Mansour Abbas joined a short-lived coalition that lasted from 2021 to 2022.He has voiced a willingness to do so again.The Joint List's Yousef Jabareen, meanwhile, has told AFP he is willing to support Eisenkot in parliament without joining his government, citing, among other concerns, the war in Gaza.Opposition division Eisenkot, 66, a former military chief and political novice, largely shares Netanyahu's views on security issues including Gaza, which Israel has reduced to rubble since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023.Eisenkot reiterated on Saturday that he would only form a 'Zionist government' whose members commit to the 'recognition of Israel as a Jewish, democratic and liberal state' and to the 'recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organisation', conditions that Arab leaders have previously refused to accept.While he has said he does not want a government dependent on Arab lists, Eisenkot has not explicitly rejected their external support.'I want them (the opposition bloc) to go ahead to be brave and do the right thing,' said demonstrator Sharon Balaban, 55, a video artist in Jerusalem.Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats has enthusiastically supported the prospect of a government backed by Arab parties, saying it would be racist to exclude them, and on Thursday met Abbas.But Avigdor Liberman, leader of the right-wing anti-Netanyahu Yisrael Beitenu party, has said he will not enter a coalition that relies on Arab parties, even for external support.'Whoever wants to rely on supporters of terrorism, let them. Yisrael Beiteinu will not be there,' he wrote on Facebook on Friday.Arabs 'are for Hamas' On the sidelines of the demonstration in Tel Aviv, more than 100 Netanyahu supporters staged a counter-protest.'It's the Right, or Palestine,' they chanted, repeating a slogan from Netanyahu's campaign.'The two Arab parties are for Hamas', said Rebecca Schindler, 60. 'They want to make Israel an Arab country.'Nava Rehavia, 70, called on Eisenkot and Liberman to join a Netanyahu-led coalition and said: 'The Arabs did not win, because they stole the election.'Netanyahu sought to raise allegations of electoral fraud during voting day, saying Arab parties had been caught with envelopes of cash.Police said they had arrested three suspects, but the election commission described the incident as an isolated local case.Netanyahu later raised allegations that Arab politicians improperly received support from Qatar.Collaboration with Arab parties would be 'a disaster for Israel', Netanyahu posted on social media on Saturday.President Isaac Herzog is expected to grant a party leader a mandate to form a government within 28 days by Thursday, with a possible 14-day extension.The negotiations come as Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump have hinted at a new attack on Iran, which could help Netanyahu run out the clock until new elections.
